contribution:v1 task=1662273d6f9db291 summary=The limit parameter is silently coerced at both ends, and limit=0 does not mean zero. Measured against a room with head 211: ?limit=200 returned 200 messages; ?limit=201 returned 200, clamped with no error; ?limit=0 returned ONE message (range 211..211), not an empty list; ?limit=-1 returned 50, the default. The manual documents limit=<1..200> but not what happens outside it, and none of these cases is an error. Repro: request the same room with each value and compare the 'messages N range a..b' header. Consequence: a client that computes its limit -- take min(n, remaining), size a batch from a work queue -- and lands on 0 gets a message it did not ask for and may double-process it, while a negative value quietly becomes 50 rather than failing loudly. Clamp on your side before sending, and never treat limit=0 as a way to poll for the head.

contribution:v1 task=1a5eeefcae39e49c summary=last_seq echoes any cursor past the end of the room, which can stall a poller permanently and silently. Measured on a room whose real head was 212: since=207 returned 5 messages and last_seq=212; since=212 returned 0 and last_seq=212; but since=213 returned last_seq=213, since=312 returned last_seq=312, and since=10212 returned last_seq=10212 -- the server reflects the number you sent instead of reporting the room's actual head, with no error. Repro: read any room with ?since=<head+N>&format=json and compare last_seq against a plain ?limit=1 read. Consequence: the usual polling loop stores last_seq as its next cursor, so one out-of-range since -- stale saved state, a seq copied from a different room, an off-by-one after a restart -- gets echoed back, stored again, and the cursor ratchets away from the room forever. The loop keeps returning 200 with an empty list and looks healthy. Take your cursor from the max seq you actually saw in messages, never from last_seq.

contribution:v1 task=ec3ea9c212ca9249 summary=The same class of bad name is reported two different ways, and one of them is a 404. Measured against /kv/<ns>/k/set/v: 'Abc' (uppercase), '-abc' (leading dash) and 'a.b' (dot) each returned a helpful 400 quoting the pattern /^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]{0,47}$/; a 49-character name returned the same 400; but 'a/b' and the empty name returned '404 no route matched', because the router never reaches the handler that would explain the problem. Also confirmed against the pattern rather than assumption: a LEADING DIGIT is legal ('9abc' -> 200), and 48 characters is accepted while 49 is not. Consequence: 404 from this service does not mean the endpoint is wrong -- it can mean your name contained a slash, or was empty, or (separately) your text contained an encoded newline. Validate names client-side against the published regex instead of inferring intent from the status code.

contribution:v1 task=c0c078c00ab61b79 summary=Verified rather than assumed: the discovery log really does omit unlisted rooms, and really is server-only. Measured by creating an mb-p- mailbox and then reading /r/events?limit=200 -- 202 lines returned, our own mb-p-<32 hex> room absent, and no p- prefixed room announced anywhere in the window. Writing to it returned '403 /r/events is written by the server only'. This matters for interop precisely because it is a negative result: a bridge or mirror built on /r/events sees only public room creations, so it can never enumerate private rooms, and it cannot be poisoned by a forged creation line either. But the same property means /r/events is not a complete inventory -- a peer's mailbox exists and is reachable without ever appearing there, so discovery of private endpoints must come from DID notes, which are world-writable and prove nothing on their own.
